papers.title: Stress Regulation through Precursor Chemistry: From Synthesis to Cycling Stability in O3‐Type Layered Oxide Cathodes
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Layered oxide cathode materials have broad application prospects in sodium‐ion batteries. However, conventional oxide solid‐state synthesis route, transition metal oxides slowly participate in the reaction step by step, causing residual stress accumulation and cycling degradation. Herein, a synthesis strategy utilizing low‐melting‐point metal salt precursors is proposed. Leveraging their synchronous decomposition and liquid‐like characteristics, a uniform chemical environment is generated, fundamentally suppressing the uneven accumulation of residual stress. Thermal analysis and kinetic calculations demonstrated that the reaction activation energy of the metal salt system (NFM‐A) was significantly reduced and exhibited a more stable variation profile. This effectively circumvented the asynchronous reaction process caused by diffusion kinetic differences inherent to the traditional oxide route (NFM‐O). Multiple experimental characterizations consistently confirmed that the residual stress of NFM‐A was low and uniformly distributed. After prolonged cycling, NFM‐A maintained a uniform lattice strain distribution with complete and dense particle morphology, while continuous stress concentration, interlayer slip, and particle cracking occurred in NFM‐O. Combined with in situ XRD and finite element simulations, the critical role of the initial stress distribution in maintaining structural integrity during electrochemical cycling is revealed. This establishes stress regulation as a key criterion for designing layered oxide cathode materials with high structural stability.

papers.title: Bulky Molecules Tailor Solvent Packing Fraction of Electrolytes for High‐Voltage Sodium‐Ion Battery
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT High‐voltage sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) suffer from rapid degradation caused by electrolyte oxidation and interfacial parasitic reactions, which are strongly influenced by the local solvation environment near the electrode surface. However, conventional electrolyte design focuses on tuning Na + –solvent interactions while overlooking solvent packing within the solvation shell. Herein, we reveal that a bulky molecular solvent mediates restricted solvent packing around Na + , with its reduced packing efficiency quantitatively described by the fractal dimension ( D f ). The enlarged molecular volume creates a more open solvation environment, facilitating anion participation and promoting ion clusters dominated by contact ion pairs (CIPs) and small aggregates (SAGGs). The resulting inorganic‐rich interphase suppresses electrolyte oxidation and interfacial parasitic reactions, enabling stable high‐voltage operation. Sodium iron sulfate (NFS) paired with the bulky‐solvent electrolyte retains 80% capacity over 1407 cycles at 1 C. An Ah‐level HC||NFS pouch cell retains 81.53% capacity after 500 cycles. A practical pouch cell further achieves 115.05 Wh kg −1 and retains 80.87% of its capacity after 150 cycles. This work demonstrates that restricted solvent packing can modulate ion association and interfacial chemistry, providing a molecular design consideration for high‐energy SIBs.
